topStories.headline: Dogpatch Data Center Permit Frozen as SF's 45-Day Moratorium Review Enters Critical Phase
topStories.dek: A citywide halt on new data center construction is now three weeks in, with a 160,000-square-foot Dogpatch project at 1215 Michigan Street caught in limbo while city planners study environmental impacts.
topStories.body:
San Francisco's Board of Supervisors voted unanimously on October 6 to impose a 45-day moratorium on approving new data centers citywide — and the clock on that freeze is now running through mid-November, with the San Francisco Planning Commission tasked with assessing whether existing and proposed facilities pose unacceptable environmental or public-health risks to nearby communities.

The measure was authored by District 10 Supervisor Shamann Walton, whose district encompasses Dogpatch, Potrero Hill and Bayview-Hunters Point — neighborhoods that host or are slated to host a disproportionate share of the city's data center infrastructure. Walton cited the city's outdated 2001 zoning codes, which predate the current AI-driven surge in computing demand, as a central justification. "We cannot use 2001 rules to regulate 2026 technology," he told reporters at City Hall.

Directly in the moratorium's path is a permitted but unbuilt 160,000-square-foot data center at 1215 Michigan Street in Dogpatch. No construction had begun before the freeze took effect. If the Planning Commission finds sufficient cause during its review, the moratorium can be extended — potentially to as long as 22 months — which could put the Dogpatch project on indefinite hold. A separate facility had launched a first phase last summer; further expansion of that site is also stalled for now.

The measure was co-sponsored by supervisors Connie Chan, Jackie Fielder and Cheyenne Chen. Oakland's City Council adopted its own 45-day data center moratorium the same week, part of a growing national trend. Walton, who is terming out in January, has framed the moratorium as a first step toward permanent restrictions. The Planning Commission study is expected to conclude before mid-November.

topStories.headline: Mission Bay's Last Undeveloped Parks Blocks Move Closer to Design, with Skate Amenities on the Table
topStories.dek: A community meeting on October 27 and an active public survey are shaping plans for the final three blocks of Mission Bay Commons and a new active recreation complex on the neighborhood's remaining open parcels.
topStories.body:
The last undeveloped parks parcels in Mission Bay moved a step closer to permanent design this week, as San Francisco Recreation & Parks and the Mission Bay Development Group held a community meeting on Tuesday, October 27, to present options and gather input from residents.

At issue are three blocks currently serving as temporary pop-up space — hosting mini golf, a food truck park and a soccer field — and a planned active recreation complex on land bordered by Mission Bay Drive, Mission Bay Circle, 7th Street and Owens Street. City planners are paying particular attention to what kind of skate and roll infrastructure residents want in the new space, with an online survey still open for public response. Rec & Park's October update identifies parcels P9 and P7 as the most likely locations for a skate-focused facility.

The Office of Community Investment and Infrastructure and the Mission Bay Development Group are responsible for developing the parks, which represent the final piece of a buildout that has already delivered multiple waterfront parks to the neighborhood. Information and the survey link are available on the Rec Park Mission Bay Future Parks Project webpage.

topStories.headline: SOMArts Opens 27th Annual Día de Los Muertos Show Honoring Mothers and Acts of Care
topStories.dek: Now open through November 20 at 934 Brannan Street, 'In Their Name' brings together altars, installations and community art centering the ancestral memory carried by mothers across generations.
topStories.body:
SOMArts Cultural Center opened its 27th annual Día de Los Muertos exhibition on October 24, marking one of the first major Day of the Dead shows of the season in San Francisco. This year's exhibition, 'In Their Name: Día de Los Muertos 2026,' was curated by Bridgètt Rex and Rio Yañez and centers on mothering as an act of care, love and political resistance.

The show runs through November 20 and features altars, mixed-media installations and community works by artists including Monique Lopez, Pin@y Educational Partnerships, Ella SF, Jonn Carlo Segovia Menchaca and Art Forces, among others. In keeping with Día de los Muertos tradition, the exhibition also includes personal altars dedicated to loved ones who have passed. Admission to the gallery during regular hours is free and open to all ages.

The show carries on a tradition founded by the late San Francisco artist and activist René Yañez. His son, curator Rio Yañez, has continued the annual exhibition since René's death in 2018, bringing in new co-curators each year. This year's theme asks how acts of nurturing can sustain communities and fuel resistance across generations. The closing reception on November 20 will feature a Día de Los Muertos Drag Show from 6 to 9 p.m. SOMArts has noted it is working to close a budget gap this year, and donations are welcome alongside ticket purchases for evening events.

moreNews.headline: Dogpatch Resident Dennis Herrera Profiled as SFPUC Departure Approaches
moreNews.body: The October issue of the Potrero View profiles longtime Dogpatch resident Dennis Herrera ahead of his planned December retirement as general manager of the San Francisco Public Utilities Commission. Herrera served as the city's elected City Attorney from 2002 to 2021 — the first Latino to hold that office — before being appointed to lead the SFPUC in late 2021. Mayor Daniel Lurie will nominate a successor, and that choice is expected to carry significant weight for the city's ongoing push toward a public power utility to replace PG&E.

moreNews.headline: Mission Bay Office Rents Hit a Record High as SoMa Rates Jump 32 Percent in a Year
moreNews.body: A third-quarter market report from CBRE, published by The Registry on October 15, found that asking rents in the Mission Bay and China Basin submarket reached a record $130.90 per square foot, while South of Market asking rents climbed 32 percent year over year. The figures reflect tightening supply of large office blocks driven significantly by AI companies consolidating space. AI startup Sierra expanded its footprint at 185 Berry Street in Mission Bay to roughly 350,000 square feet during Q3, cementing its position as one of the building's anchor tenants.
